Request a hypothesis on how to navigate this temperature window to form a dense, single-phase-like microstructure that maximizes barrier properties. Include prior evidence on the limitations of standard sintering in this regime, define the boundary where density fails or volatility occurs, and propose a falsification experiment comparing intermediate temperatures against the proposed optimum.

There is a shared understanding that interface coherence (via specific crystallographic relationships) and aging temperature regimes are not arbitrary but are selected to probe specific mechanisms governing ductility and phase transformation. Paper PMC11087546 adopts a structural characterization approach, selecting the Kurdjumov–Sachs (KS) relationship ((01-1)B2//(−111)FCC) as a definitive criterion to confirm high coherency at the interface, linking this directly to interfacial energy reduction and ductility. The efficacy of the KS relationship as a coherency marker is dependent on the specific B2/FCC phase pair interaction in the Al0.7CoCrFeNi system under ambient conditions [1]. The selection of the 520–1200 °C temperature regime is condition-dependent on the material's susceptibility to dynamic evolution of local chemical order (LCO) and phase boundary (PB) configurations, which triggers plastic instability specifically in the intermediate regime [2]. Neither paper fully integrates the kinetics of phase transformation over time (e.g., the specific 5-minute stabilization time mentioned in the query variants) with the long-term aging regimes or the exact boundaries where the KS relationship might deviate during the dynamic evolution of LCO described in the aging study.
